summary:
Crop Compass is a friendly second opinion for farmers deciding what to plant next.

Farmers already face dry spells, hot summers and surprise frosts, and most tools just hand them charts. Crop Compass reads NASA’s records and explains what they mean in plain language.

Pick a place and you see how much water has been in the soil month by month, and which months ran dry. You can slide the weather to try a dry or hot year. It then walks you through a few crop rotations, scores each one with a likely range, and shows the trade-offs. After every chart, a short “in plain words” box says why we say it and what it could mean for you. You can save the result as a one-page plan.

It uses NASA POWER weather and soil-wetness data, plus MODIS satellite greenness and imagery. We tested the model on years it never saw, and it beat a plain “usual year” guess in all three places. We also state its limits openly.

Crop Compass doesn’t make the decision. It helps farmers see their season more clearly, so they can adapt with more confidence.
details:
What it does / how it works
Crop Compass is a website that gives farmers a second opinion on their next crop. Pick the place closest to your farm, see how much water was in the soil each month (dry months get flagged), then slide the weather around to try a dry or hot year. Answer 4 quick questions about what matters to you and it ranks a few crop rotations with a score, a likely range and the trade-offs. Every chart has a plain-words box: why we say it, what it could mean for you. You can save it all as a one-page plan.

Under the hood, a gradient boosting model learns how weather turns into soil wetness. Conformal prediction puts uncertainty ranges around it. Rotation scores come from simple crop-trait rules, run through 400 weather variations.

Benefits

  • NASA data turned into advice farmers can actually read, not just charts
  • Shows uncertainty and trade-offs, not one “right” answer
  • Free, opens in any browser, no login

Intended impact
Help farmers see dry months, heat and frost coming before they plant, and adapt with more confidence. It supports their judgment, doesn’t replace it.

Tools / tech

  • NASA POWER (weather and soil wetness, 2015–2025), MODIS NDVI greenness, MODIS imagery via NASA GIBS
  • Python for data and the model, HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the site
  • Hosted on Netlify
  • Code maintenance and building on GitHub

What’s creative

  • Plain-words box after every chart
  • Three-ring “compass” showing dry months, hot days and frost years at a glance
  • Honest about its weak spots
  • Friendly greeting and casual tone, made for farmers

What we considered

  • Advisory only: farmers know their own land
  • Honesty about limits: soil wetness is an estimate, not field probes; crop traits are rules of thumb; no prices yet
  • It beat a “usual year” guess on unseen years in all 3 places, but our 80% ranges only held 72% in Iowa and 64% in Kansas, and the site says that
  • Used only data with no login, so SMAP and GPM are next steps
  • Simple wording, readable layout, dark mode
dataRefs: NASA POWER: daily rain, temperature, humidity, sunlight and soil wetness (2015–2025)
MODIS Terra vegetation index, MOD13Q1 (NDVI plant greenness)
NASA ORNL DAAC MODIS subsets (how we pulled the NDVI for each place)
NASA GIBS / Worldview: MODIS natural-colour and greenness satellite images
